title: Four AirTags Later: What Actually Works (and What Doesn't)
metaDescription: Real-world testing of Apple's AirTag 4-pack after months of daily use. Here's what works well and the limitations you should know about.
content:
## The plastic feels cheaper than expected, but it's surprisingly durable

The white plastic housing looks clean but doesn't feel premium when you first handle it. After dropping one down concrete stairs and finding another in my washing machine, they're tougher than they appear. The metal back with Apple logo adds some weight, though these are still lighter than I anticipated.

## Setup lives up to the one-tap promise

Hold an AirTag near your iPhone and it pops up immediately. Tap connect, name it, and you're done in about 30 seconds per tag. The process works exactly as advertised - no app downloads, no account creation, just tap and go. I had all four connected in under three minutes.

## Precision Finding works great indoors

The Ultra Wideband feature is genuinely helpful when you're close to your lost item. Point your phone around the room and it shows distance plus direction arrows. Found my keys buried in couch cushions and my wallet wedged between car seats using this. The accuracy gets you within a few inches, and the interface is intuitive.

## Range limitations become obvious quickly

AirTags work through Apple's Find My network, which means they need other Apple devices nearby to report location. In dense urban areas, this works well. My backpack showed up accurately when I left it at a coffee shop downtown. But in rural areas or places with fewer iPhones around, location updates can be sparse or hours old.

## Battery life exceeds the one-year claim

My first batch has been running for 14 months on the original CR2032 batteries. The Find My app shows battery levels, and mine are still at 40-60%. Replacing the battery is simple - twist off the back, pop in a new one. Standard coin cell batteries work fine, no special Apple version needed.

## Privacy features work as intended

If someone else's AirTag travels with you, your iPhone alerts you after a few hours. The AirTag also starts beeping after being separated from its owner for extended periods. These anti-stalking measures work, though the beeping can be loud enough to annoy people nearby.

## Real-world accuracy varies by situation

In my house, AirTags pinpoint items within a room or two. Outside, GPS accuracy through the Find My network gets you to the right building or area. Don't expect street-address precision if your item is truly lost in a large area. The crowd-sourced location updates depend entirely on nearby Apple devices.

## Works best for frequently misplaced items

These excel at finding things you lose around the house or in familiar places. Keys, wallets, bags - stuff that gets set down and forgotten. They're less useful for true theft protection since someone can disable them fairly easily. Think daily convenience rather than security device.

## The silent mode creates a real problem

You can make AirTags play a sound through the Find My app, but only if your phone has an internet connection. No connection means no sound, which defeats the purpose when you need it most. The beeping also isn't very loud - hard to hear if your item is in another room or buried under things.
pros: Genuinely simple one-tap setup process with iPhone
Precision Finding with Ultra Wideband works accurately indoors
Battery lasts well over a year with normal use
Durable construction despite lightweight plastic feel
Privacy features prevent unwanted tracking effectively
Uses standard CR2032 batteries, easy to replace
Integrates seamlessly with existing Find My app
cons: Range depends entirely on nearby Apple devices for location updates
Sound alerts require internet connection to activate
Limited effectiveness in rural areas with fewer iPhones
Plastic construction feels less premium than expected
verdict: AirTags work well for everyday item tracking if you live in areas with decent iPhone density. They're convenient for keys and wallets but aren't a replacement for serious security devices.
targetAudience: iPhone users who frequently misplace items around the house or in urban areas with good Apple device coverage
